title: My Daily Brief
overview: A nationwide FAA ground stop halted US air travel for hours on Friday. Officials blamed aging equipment and said there was no sign of a cyberattack, and they used the moment to press Congress for modernization money. The Nvidia scandal widened into a public dispute inside the Trump cabinet. Also in this edition: a challenge to Chuck Schumer's Senate leadership, Microsoft's global outage, a cruise boat collision in New Orleans, and a planned Trump–Xi–Putin meeting.

stories.headline: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop; officials blame old equipment, not a cyberattack
stories.summary: The FAA lifted a nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, about four hours after communication and radar problems led it to halt departures. At a White House briefing, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said overloaded routers in an 'incredibly old' air traffic control system went down, and he warned that recovery would be slow. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack and no link to the concurrent Microsoft outage, though agencies had not ruled anything out. Both officials used the briefing to urge Congress to fund a new air traffic control system. Disruptions are expected to carry into the weekend.
key_facts: The ground stop began just before 4 p.m. ET Friday and was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET.
Duffy said more than 3,500 planes were airborne when the stop was issued; by 8 p.m. ET fewer than 400 remained in the air.
FlightAware counted roughly 10,500 or more delays and about 3,580 cancellations.
Duffy said the FAA did not lose all radar or communications, and medevac and law enforcement flights continued.
ASI, the contractor rolling out the FAA's new AI-based 'Smart' tool, said the ground stop was not caused by its system.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian stressed travel chaos and described the briefing as quickly turning into a funding plea. It quoted Democrats Gavin Newsom and Ro Khanna criticizing the administration's communication, along with frustrated passengers. It also noted Mullin's suggestion that new technology may have overwhelmed the older system, and CNN's report that the trouble began at Chicago Midway.

AFP, via the Korea Herald, and Axios focused on the official explanation: old hardware, no cyberattack, and the request to Congress for funding. AFP also noted that Trump had not commented hours into the disruption, and that officials defended him on this.

Fox Business and the Washington Examiner gave a detailed timeline built on Duffy's account and his emphasis on caution and safety. They highlighted the funding request and noted that the FAA had not ruled out a cyberattack. Fox included ASI's statement denying any role.

disputed: The exact root cause: Duffy described overloaded routers, while Mullin suggested new equipment overwhelmed the old system. Duffy denied that the new Smart system was responsible.
The size of the funding request: AFP reported a $30 billion request made the previous day, while Fox Business reported Duffy now seeking $50 billion in emergency funding.
Whether a cyberattack has been fully ruled out: officials said there is no evidence of one, but investigations are continuing.
stories.why: A failure that grounded the entire US air system raises questions about the reliability of aviation infrastructure and is likely to shape a major funding fight in Congress.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns amid affair reports and spy concerns; board seeks successor
stories.summary: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday after reports of several extramarital affairs. One reported relationship was with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia chips, has been investigated over suspected diversion of restricted chips to China. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the Financial Times reports that the board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, and Democrats have opened their own inquiry into the administration's handling of the matter.
key_facts: Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading Nvidia; Colette Kress is interim CEO.
Nvidia's board says it will consider internal and external candidates for permanent CEO; Arm said 'no comment' on the Haas report.
TechCrunch reported that Megaspeed bought about $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips over two years.
Senate Banking chair Tim Scott has asked Huang and Lutnick to testify; Lutnick is scheduled for next month.
The New York Times reported that Trump called Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian focused on political accountability, especially pressure on Lutnick and Trump's ties to Huang. It quoted Democrats Schumer and Jeffries as well as Republicans Curtis and Cornyn ('Heads should roll'), and cited AP reporting that White House officials were discussing whether Lutnick should be fired.

TechCrunch built a detailed timeline that included the national security stakes and reports of Huang's state of mind. CNBC looked back at Nvidia's history and the stakes for its AI dominance. Newsweek covered the viral AI-generated memes and quoted a misinformation expert.

Fox Business concentrated on corporate succession: the FT report on Rene Haas, Kress's appointment, and the board's praise for Huang's contributions. Its coverage was largely free of the political accountability angle.

disputed: The claim that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy rests on reported suspicions of US officials and has not been proven.
Nvidia, Huang and Kimberly Powell have not confirmed the reported affair with Powell; a further Reuters report of another affair cites an unnamed employee.
Estimates of chip volumes differ: $4.8 billion purchased by Megaspeed (TechCrunch) versus at least $7.5 billion moved to Chinese firms (The Information, via the Daily Caller).
What Trump and administration officials knew, and when, remains under investigation.
stories.why: A leadership crisis at the world's leading AI chipmaker touches markets, US–China tech competition, and national security policy all at once.

stories.headline: Van Hollen launches challenge to Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he will challenge Chuck Schumer for leader of Senate Democrats, who take the majority on January 4 after their midterm wins. Van Hollen said voters 'chose change,' called for new leadership, and backed ending the filibuster. Schumer said he welcomes the discussion and has the votes to stay on. The secret-ballot vote is expected in early December.
key_facts: The winner needs 28 votes, or 29 if Democrats win Alaska's Senate race.
Bernie Sanders, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan back Van Hollen.
Senators Jacky Rosen and Kirsten Gillibrand back Schumer.
Schumer has led Senate Democrats since 2017; Fox reports there has been no contested Democratic leadership election since 1994.
Van Hollen said he is no longer pursuing a possible 2028 presidential bid.

perspectives.framing: PBS analyzed the vote math and concluded that Schumer has the advantage, while noting that many newly elected senators oppose him. The Guardian ran an op-ed by Bernie Sanders casting the race as a choice between establishment politics and a grassroots, working-class agenda.
The BBC, Axios and The Hill presented the race as a test of Democratic divisions. They quoted endorsements on both sides and noted that Schumer remains the favorite.
Fox News called it a 'progressive rebellion,' reporting from a Denver Democratic conference. It highlighted Van Hollen's pledge to end the filibuster and quoted activists calling for Schumer to go.

disputed: Whether Schumer actually has the votes: he says he does, but PBS reports he lacks a public majority of pledges.
Alaska's Senate race between Mary Peltola and Dan Sullivan is still being counted, which affects the vote threshold.
stories.why: The outcome will shape how the new Democratic majority uses its power, including on the filibuster and its approach to Trump.

stories.headline: Microsoft apologizes for global outage, cites network change
stories.summary: A Microsoft 365 outage hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other services for millions of users in more than 70 countries, lasting roughly a day or more before recovery began. Microsoft said it was 'deeply sorry' and blamed an issue from an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. The company said the problem was not related to cyberattacks or AI agents. Courts, hospitals, police forces and government offices were affected in several countries. Microsoft says it will publish a full post-incident report.
key_facts: Microsoft said the outage was 'a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.'
The company said services were restored gradually to ensure stability, with some users still facing intermittent issues and delayed email.
Maine's courts warned that protection-order requests filed by email might not have been received.
In Australia, some health facilities returned to paper scripts; UK police forces asked the public to phone instead of reporting crimes online.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian emphasized the economic damage and dependence on foreign technology, quoting Australian experts who warned of billion-dollar costs and closures of small businesses. PBS ran an explainer on why email outages take longer to recover from. The Verge reported a sourced link to Azure network configuration changes.
The BBC, Axios and The Hill focused on the scale of the disruption, Microsoft's statements, and vulnerabilities for courts and governments.

disputed: The precise technical cause awaits Microsoft's post-incident report; the Azure VNet link comes from a Verge correspondent's sources.
Reports differ on timing, with start dates given as Thursday, November 12 or Friday depending on time zone, and some services still degraded.
Australian cost estimates in the billions are expert projections.
stories.why: The outage showed how much of daily business and government depends on a single provider's software.

stories.headline: Bessent says Commerce held up blacklisting of Nvidia customer Megaspeed
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that Treasury, War, USTR and State had favored adding Megaspeed to the US entity list 'for months,' but that 'Commerce has the pen.' The comment directed scrutiny at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Bessent said he was frustrated by chip 'leakage' to China. He also said the real story was whether Nvidia properly vetted its customers. Lutnick is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.
key_facts: Bessent: 'Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen.'
Bessent said Trump made clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s.
Megaspeed is not on the entity list.
A Commerce spokesperson denied that a reported conversation between Bessent and Lutnick took place; Bessent said, 'We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room.'

perspectives.framing: PBS framed the story as a public fight between Trump advisers. It highlighted Lutnick's closeness to Huang and recounted the history of export controls, including the Commerce Department's 2025 decision to drop a Biden-era chip rule, with analysis from a former Biden NSC official.
The BBC, Axios and The Hill described a rare public rift in the cabinet. They noted past Bessent–Lutnick tensions and gave weight to Bessent's point that Nvidia's own oversight should be examined.

The Daily Caller used pointed language ('Throws Lutnick Under The Bus,' 'Chip Export Fiasco') and cited The Information's $7.5 billion figure. It described Huang as having shipped chips to China following the relationship.

disputed: Whether Bessent and Lutnick had the reported Situation Room exchange; Commerce denies it.
Whether Megaspeed diverted advanced chips to China, and how many, remains under investigation.
Whether Nvidia knew or should have known that it was selling to pass-through companies.
stories.why: The dispute could determine who in the administration is held accountable for advanced US chips reaching China.

stories.headline: Tanker strikes docked river cruise boat in New Orleans; 32 hospitalized, no deaths
stories.summary: The tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked paddlewheel cruise boat American Heritage on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday at about 12:30 p.m. The impact caused the cruise boat to tip over and partly sink while passengers were disembarking. All passengers and crew were accounted for, and 32 people were hospitalized, none critically. Mayor Helena Moreno called it 'a miracle on the Mississippi.' The cause is under investigation.
key_facts: 129 passengers were aboard; Axios cites about 180 people in total including crew.
32 people were hospitalized, none with critical injuries, and no deaths were reported.
The mayor said the tanker 'lost control and collided into the cruise ship.'
The 160-meter, Marshall Islands–flagged tanker carries asphalt and bitumen.
The river was closed to vessel traffic.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera and PBS gave straightforward accounts that drew on official figures, details about the vessels, and witness quotes.
DW, Axios and a CBS affiliate emphasized the rescue, the mayor's 'miracle' remark, and eyewitness accounts.
The Daily Caller covered the early rescue with embedded social media posts and praised the speed of the emergency response. Its reporting came before injury figures were available.

disputed: The cause of the collision and whether the tanker was carrying cargo are unknown.
Reported totals of people aboard vary: nearly 130, 129 passengers, and about 180 including crew.
stories.why: Serious accidents on a busy commercial waterway raise questions about port safety and traffic on the river.

stories.headline: Charlotte ICE protester sentenced to five months in federal prison
stories.summary: A federal judge sentenced Heather Morrow, 45, a Charlotte school bus driver, to five months in prison followed by seven months of supervised release. The charges stem from a November 2025 protest at an ICE office during 'Operation Charlotte's Web.' A jury convicted her in September of assault and other misdemeanors. Prosecutors had sought eight months. Her lawyer says she will appeal, and she reports to prison on January 13, 2027.
key_facts: Judge Matthew E. Orso imposed five months in prison plus seven months of supervised release.
Prosecutors had asked for eight months.
Co-defendant William Stanley received one year of probation last month.
Morrow apologized in court.

perspectives.framing: WFAE (NPR) gave a brief factual report that noted Morrow's job, her unsuccessful run for county commissioner, and her planned appeal.

Local TV outlets presented both sides: the US Attorney's Office called the case interference with law enforcement, not protected speech, while supporters said the government wanted to make an example of her.

disputed: Supporters argue that the sentence was meant to send a message; prosecutors say it reflects the crime. An appeal is planned.
stories.why: The case is an early test of how federal courts sentence protesters at immigration enforcement sites.

stories.headline: FAA grounds all US flights for first time since 2023
stories.summary: This is early coverage of Friday's FAA ground stop, issued over communication problems at the 22 regional air traffic control centers. It was only the second nationwide stop since the 9/11 attacks. Homeland Security Secretary Mullin said there was no sign yet of a nefarious act. Hundreds of flights were diverted, and the disruption spread to US-bound flights from Australia.
key_facts: The previous nationwide ground stop was in January 2023.
Cirium counted at least 827 diversions as of 7:05 p.m. EST.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart after 4 p.m. EST.
Some flights within Alaska and Hawaii were unaffected.

perspectives.framing: PBS carried AP's report focused on stranded travelers and official reassurances. The Guardian covered delays at Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.
The Korea Herald ran the same AP-based account, with passenger stories and diversion statistics.

disputed: The cause was still under investigation when these reports were written; see the related story on the ground stop being lifted.
stories.why: It shows how a single US system failure can spread to international travel.

stories.headline: Trump to meet Xi and Putin together in China next week
stories.summary: The White House said Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will hold the first-ever three-way meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders on Thursday, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Officials said Trump will raise reducing nuclear arsenals and the war in Iran. Ukraine is not expected to be discussed, and neither are the Nvidia scandal or chip export controls. Trump will first attend an ASEAN summit in the Philippines, and a US official said there are no plans to engage North Korea.
key_facts: The meeting is scheduled for Thursday in Shenzhen, alongside APEC.
Trump will also hold a bilateral lunch and meeting with Xi, their fourth meeting since his return to office; no separate meeting with Putin is planned.
Elon Musk will accompany Trump but will not join the trilateral meeting.
Trump leaves Washington Monday for the Philippines.

perspectives.framing: CNA detailed the agenda from White House officials. Yonhap and the Korea Herald focused on the absence of North Korea engagement and framed the meeting in the context of efforts to end the Ukraine war.

disputed: Yonhap and the Korea Herald link the meeting to Ukraine diplomacy, while US officials told CNA that Ukraine will not be discussed there.
stories.why: An unprecedented meeting of the three nuclear powers could affect arms control and several ongoing conflicts.

stories.headline: Charlotte-born QB Sam Hartman named star of 'The Bachelor' season 30
stories.summary: ABC named Washington Commanders backup quarterback Sam Hartman, a 27-year-old Charlotte native, as the lead of The Bachelor's 30th season. The show returns after a two-year hiatus, with a premiere on March 21. Hartman previously played at Wake Forest and Notre Dame.
key_facts: The season premieres March 21 (2027) on ABC and streams on Hulu.
Hartman threw for 12,967 yards and 110 touchdowns at Wake Forest.

perspectives.framing: Charlotte outlets emphasized his local roots.
The Daily Caller focused on his football career and on past athlete Bachelors.

stories.why: It is a light local-interest story for Charlotte readers.
